content: In biological terms, the cuticle, also known as the cuticula, refers to various tough yet flexible, non-mineralized outer coverings of an organism or parts of an organism that serve a protective function. These structures are not homologous, meaning they differ in their origin, structure, and chemical composition. In human anatomy, the term cuticle is used to describe the dead layers of epidermal cells or keratinocytes that produce the horn protein keratin. It also refers to the strip of dead skin cells located at the base and sides of the fingernail, known as the eponychium. Additionally, the term applies to the superficial layer of overlapping cells that cover the hair shaft, known as the cuticula pili, which helps anchor the hair within its follicle. In invertebrate zoology, the cuticle or cuticula is a multi-layered structure found outside the epidermis of many invertebrates, such as roundworms and arthropods, where it forms an exoskeleton. In nematodes, the primary structural components of the cuticle include proteins, highly cross-linked collagens, and specialized insoluble proteins called cuticlins, along with glycoproteins and lipids. In arthropods, the main structural component of the cuticle is chitin, a polysaccharide composed of N-acetylglucosamine units, which is combined with proteins and lipids. In botany, plant cuticles are protective waxy coverings produced by the epidermal cells of leaves, young shoots, and other aerial plant organs. The primary structural components of plant cuticles are unique polymers such as cutin and/or cutan, which are impregnated with wax. These cuticles function as permeability barriers, preventing the loss of water and water-soluble materials. They also prevent plant surfaces from becoming wet and help reduce desiccation. Xerophytic plants, such as cacti, possess very thick cuticles to adapt to their arid environments. Similarly, plants exposed to sea spray often have thicker cuticles to protect against the toxic effects of salt.
